name: Hysteria and the vibrator
when: Hysteria diagnosis: ancient to 1980; electric vibrator: 1880s
summary: For more than 2,000 years doctors blamed a wide range of women's complaints — anxiety, fainting, irritability, sleeplessness, even too much or too little desire — on a single 'disease' called hysteria, from the Greek hystera, 'womb'. Victorian doctors diagnosed it constantly, and the electric vibrator was invented in the same era. A popular story links the two: that doctors 'treated' hysteria by bringing women to orgasm by hand, and invented the vibrator to save their tired wrists. The truth is messier and more interesting.
story: Hippocratic and later Galenic writers imagined the womb wandering around the body or 'suffocating' when a woman was not regularly having sex or babies; their cure was marriage, pregnancy, scents, and sometimes genital massage by a midwife. In the 19th century hysteria became a catch-all diagnosis for women who did not fit expectations, studied theatrically by Jean-Martin Charcot in Paris and later by Sigmund Freud. In 1880s London the doctor Joseph Mortimer Granville patented an electromechanical 'percusser' — the first electric vibrator. By the 1900s vibrators were sold openly in Sears catalogues and women's magazines as health and beauty 'massagers' that relieved 'nervousness', years before electric irons and vacuum cleaners were common. When they appeared in early pornographic films in the 1920s, respectable advertising dried up.
truth: The famous version comes from historian Rachel Maines's 1999 book The Technology of Orgasm, which inspired the play In the Next Room and the film Hysteria (2011). In 2018 historians Hallie Lieberman and Eric Schatzberg checked her sources and found almost no evidence that Victorian doctors routinely gave patients orgasms; Granville himself wrote that he used his device on men's muscles and specifically not on women for hysteria. So: hysteria was real as a (largely invented) diagnosis, early vibrators were real and openly sold as 'health' devices, but the image of rich women queuing at the doctor for orgasm treatment is largely a modern myth built on thin evidence.
reshaped: Hysteria showed how medicine could turn women's ordinary emotions and frustrations into a disease, and was used to deny women votes, education and control over their lives. It was only removed from the American psychiatric manual (DSM) in 1980. The vibrator, rebranded from medical device to personal product after the 1960s feminist movement, became the core of a global sexual-wellness industry worth tens of billions of dollars a year.
industry: The 'massager' market of the 1900s became today's sexual wellness industry, estimated at well over $30 billion a year and now sold in mainstream pharmacies.
connections: Sigmund Freud; Women's suffrage; Industrial Revolution; Electric light bulb

name: Castrati
summary: For about 300 years, thousands of Italian boys were castrated before puberty so that their voices would not break. The operation did not make the voice lower — it kept it high, like a boy's, but powered by an adult man's lungs and chest, giving a voice of extraordinary range, power and length of breath. The best castrati were the superstars of Baroque opera, and the Catholic Church used them in choirs because women were not allowed to sing in church.
story: The practice took off in the late 16th century, when the Sistine Chapel began hiring castrati. Poor families, often in southern Italy, had sons operated on in the hope of fortune; the boy was usually drugged with opium, placed in a hot bath, and the spermatic cords were cut or the testicles crushed. Because the operation was technically illegal and done secretly, nobody knows how many died from infection or bleeding, but deaths were certainly common, and most survivors never became great singers — many ended up in minor church choirs. Lacking testosterone, castrati often grew unusually tall, with long limbs, smooth skin and broad chests. The greatest, like Farinelli (Carlo Broschi, 1705–1782) and Senesino, were paid fortunes, and Farinelli spent 22 years singing privately to cure the depression of King Philip V of Spain.
truth: Contemporary gossip claimed castrati were popular lovers with aristocratic women because they could not cause pregnancy; some castrati did have famous affairs, and since castration before puberty did not always remove all sexual function, this was not pure myth — but it was exaggerated in satire. Estimates of '4,000 boys a year' at the peak, often quoted, come from 18th-century guesses and are probably too high. Alessandro Moreschi, the last castrato of the Sistine Chapel, was recorded on gramophone in 1902–1904 — the only recordings of a castrato voice that exist.
reshaped: The castrati shaped Baroque music: Handel, Vivaldi and Mozart wrote leading roles for them, and many 'heroic' male roles were written for high voices — today sung by women or countertenors. Enlightenment ideas, Napoleon's rule in Italy and changing taste made the practice look barbaric; Pope Leo XIII stopped hiring new castrati in 1878, and Pius X banned them from church music in 1903.
industry: They were the first international pop stars of opera, with fan culture, huge fees and rivalries; their decline helped make women sopranos the stars of opera.
connections: Baroque; Catholic Church; George Frideric Handel; Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart; Napoleon Bonaparte; Eunuchs in imperial courts

name: Syphilis
when: First epidemic 1495; cured by penicillin from 1943
summary: Syphilis exploded across Europe in 1495 among the soldiers of King Charles VIII of France besieging Naples, and within five years it had spread from Scotland to India. It was a terrifying, disfiguring disease that could destroy the nose, bones and brain, and every nation blamed another: the Italians called it the French disease, the French the Neapolitan disease, the Russians the Polish disease and the Turks the Christian disease.
story: Because the first outbreak followed Columbus's return from the Americas in 1493, many historians believe his crews brought it back — making it part of the Columbian exchange — though some skeletons suggest it existed in Europe earlier. Treatment for 400 years was mercury, inhaled, rubbed in or swallowed, which caused teeth to fall out and often killed patients: 'a night with Venus, a lifetime with Mercury'. In 1910 Paul Ehrlich's arsenic drug Salvarsan became the first modern targeted medicine, and penicillin finally cured it in the 1940s. Suspected or known sufferers included Henry VIII (disputed), Ivan the Terrible, Al Capone, Guy de Maupassant and Friedrich Nietzsche.
truth: Syphilis is behind one of the worst medical scandals in history: in the Tuskegee study (1932–1972), the US Public Health Service watched hundreds of poor Black men with syphilis go untreated — even after penicillin was available — to study how it killed them. In Guatemala (1946–48) US researchers deliberately infected prisoners and patients. Both were exposed only decades later.
reshaped: Fear of syphilis changed behaviour across Europe: public bathhouses closed, condoms of linen and animal gut were first described (by Gabriele Falloppio in 1564) as protection against it, and governments began registering and inspecting sex workers. Its cure gave birth to modern pharmaceutical chemistry.
industry: Salvarsan made Hoechst a pharmaceutical giant and launched the idea of the 'magic bullet' drug that underpins today's drug industry.
connections: Columbian exchange; Christopher Columbus; Henry VIII; Penicillin; Tuskegee syphilis study; Contraception before the Pill

name: Contraception before the Pill
summary: People have tried to control pregnancy for at least 4,000 years. The Egyptian Kahun papyrus (c. 1850 BCE) recommends mixtures of crocodile dung and honey; Greek and Roman women used plants, the most famous being silphium, a herb from Cyrene in Libya so valued as a contraceptive that it appeared on coins — and was harvested to extinction by the 1st century CE.
story: Withdrawal, prolonged breastfeeding, abstinence and abortion were the most common methods for most of history. Condoms made of linen, then sheep or fish gut, were used in the 16th–18th centuries mainly against disease; Casanova described testing them. The big change was rubber: after Charles Goodyear vulcanised rubber in 1844, cheap rubber condoms and diaphragms were mass-produced, and latex condoms followed in the 1920s. Governments fought back: the USA's Comstock Act (1873) made it a crime to mail contraceptives or even information about them, and Margaret Sanger was arrested for opening America's first birth-control clinic in 1916.
truth: Many ancient 'remedies' were useless or poisonous, but some, like silphium and wild carrot seed, may have had real effects. Families in many parts of Europe managed to have fewer children long before modern contraception, mostly through late marriage and withdrawal.
reshaped: The ability to separate sex from pregnancy changed family size, women's education and work, and the economy. Falling birth rates in 19th-century France, and later everywhere, reshaped nations and armies.
industry: The condom industry, born from rubber vulcanisation, now produces tens of billions of condoms a year and became central to fighting HIV.
connections: Casanova; Comstock laws; Syphilis; The birth-control pill; Margaret Sanger

name: The birth-control pill
summary: The Pill was the first contraceptive a woman could take privately, reliably and independently of a man. Approved in the United States in 1960 as Enovid, it was used by millions within five years and became one of the most important inventions of the 20th century.
story: Margaret Sanger, who had campaigned for birth control since 1914, and the heiress Katharine McCormick, who funded it, recruited biologist Gregory Pincus to develop a 'magic pill'. Pincus worked with the Catholic gynaecologist John Rock and chemists who had synthesised hormones from Mexican wild yams. It was first approved only for 'menstrual disorders' — and suddenly a lot of women reported menstrual disorders. Married women in some US states could not legally get it until 1965, and unmarried women until 1972.
truth: The large trials were held in 1956 in Puerto Rico, among poor women who were not fully told it was an experimental drug or about side effects; three participants died and were never investigated. Early pills had far higher hormone doses than today's, causing blood clots. Sanger was also linked to the eugenics movement, which still clouds her legacy.
reshaped: The Pill helped drive the sexual revolution, let women delay marriage and children, stay in education and build careers, and economists link it to the large rise in women doctors and lawyers in the 1970s. The Catholic Church's 1968 rejection of it (Humanae Vitae) caused a lasting split between church teaching and many believers.
industry: Oral contraceptives became a multibillion-dollar pharmaceutical market and opened the age of 'lifestyle' drugs.
connections: Margaret Sanger; Contraception before the Pill; Sexual revolution; Catholic Church; Comstock laws

name: Viagra
summary: Viagra (sildenafil) was developed by Pfizer scientists in Sandwich, England, as a heart medicine for angina. In trials it did little for the heart, but male volunteers reported an unexpected side effect, and some reportedly refused to return their leftover pills.
story: Pfizer switched course, and Viagra was approved in the USA in March 1998, becoming one of the fastest-selling drugs in history. Former US presidential candidate Bob Dole and footballer Pelé appeared in adverts, breaking the taboo around impotence.
truth: Its arrival raised questions about whether men's sexual problems were treated more seriously than women's; a drug for women's low desire (flibanserin) was only approved in 2015, after a controversial campaign.
reshaped: Viagra made impotence a medical condition people could talk about, and it reduced demand for animal products such as tiger penis and rhino horn used in traditional medicine — though how much is debated.
industry: At its peak Viagra earned Pfizer nearly $2 billion a year and created the 'men's health' market and online pharmacy industry.
connections: Pharmaceutical industry; Hysteria and the vibrator

name: Kinsey Reports
summary: Alfred Kinsey, an Indiana University zoologist who had studied gall wasps, interviewed thousands of Americans about their sex lives and published Sexual Behavior in the Human Male (1948) and Sexual Behavior in the Human Female (1953). Both became best-sellers and shocked the country.
story: Kinsey reported that most men and many women had sex before marriage, that affairs were common, and that a large minority had some same-sex experience; he created the 0–6 'Kinsey scale' to show sexuality as a spectrum rather than two boxes. The female volume caused such outrage that his funding from the Rockefeller Foundation was cut.
truth: His samples over-represented prisoners and volunteers, so some numbers (such as '10% gay') were too high. Some data on children came from a paedophile's diaries, which has made his work deeply controversial.
reshaped: Kinsey's reports made it possible to study sex scientifically, paved the way for later researchers like Masters and Johnson, and fed the sexual revolution and gay-rights movement.
industry: Sexology became a field, leading to sex education, therapy and research institutes.
connections: Sexual revolution; Stonewall riots

name: AIDS crisis and activism
summary: In 1981 doctors in the USA reported rare pneumonias and cancers among young gay men. The new disease, AIDS, caused by HIV, turned out to have crossed from chimpanzees to humans in central Africa early in the 20th century, and it has since killed about 40 million people.
story: Governments were slow to act, partly because the first victims were gay men and drug users; US President Reagan did not speak publicly about AIDS until 1985. Activist groups such as ACT UP stormed drug-company offices and the FDA, forcing faster drug approvals. Effective combination therapy arrived in 1996, but prices kept it out of reach for most Africans until Indian generic makers like Cipla cut the cost to under a dollar a day in 2001.
truth: Conspiracy theories that the CIA created HIV were deliberately spread by the Soviet KGB in the 1980s ('Operation Infektion'). South Africa's government under Thabo Mbeki denied that HIV caused AIDS, a policy estimated to have cost over 300,000 lives.
reshaped: AIDS changed medicine (patients demanding a say in research), drug pricing and patent law, and made condoms and frank sex education mainstream. It also brought gay communities into public view and built the movement for equal rights.
industry: HIV drugs became a huge market, and India's generic industry earned the name 'pharmacy of the developing world'.
connections: HIV/AIDS pandemic; Stonewall riots; Operation Infektion; India

name: Habsburg marriage strategy
summary: 'Let others wage war; you, happy Austria, marry' was the motto attached to the Habsburgs, a family that built one of the largest empires in history largely through carefully arranged weddings rather than conquest.
story: Maximilian I married Mary of Burgundy in 1477, gaining the Netherlands; his son Philip married Joanna of Castile, heir to Spain. Their son Charles V inherited Spain, its American colonies, the Netherlands, Austria and much of Italy — an empire 'on which the sun never set'. To keep the lands in the family, Habsburgs kept marrying cousins and nieces.
truth: The inbreeding was catastrophic. The 'Habsburg jaw' became more extreme in each generation, and Charles II of Spain (1661–1700) — whose parents were uncle and niece — could barely chew or speak, was sickly and childless. A 2009 genetic study calculated his inbreeding as close to that of a child of a brother and sister.
reshaped: Charles II's death without heirs triggered the War of the Spanish Succession (1701–1714), a European world war that put the French Bourbons on Spain's throne. Royal marriages decided the borders of Europe for centuries.
connections: Charles V; Holy Roman Empire; Spanish Empire; War of the Spanish Succession

name: Henry VIII and the break with Rome
summary: Henry VIII's desperation for a son and his passion for Anne Boleyn led him to break England away from the Catholic Church — one of the clearest examples of love and lust changing the religion of a nation.
story: Henry's wife Catherine of Aragon had given him only a daughter, Mary. When the Pope refused an annulment — partly because Catherine's nephew, Emperor Charles V, controlled Rome — Henry had Parliament declare him Supreme Head of the Church of England in 1534, married Anne, and closed the monasteries, seizing their wealth. Anne gave him a daughter, Elizabeth, and was beheaded in 1536 on charges of adultery and incest that most historians think were fabricated. He married six times in all.
truth: Henry was also motivated by money and power: the dissolution of the monasteries transferred about a quarter of England's land to the crown and its supporters.
reshaped: England became Protestant, leading to centuries of religious conflict, the Anglican Church, and indirectly the colonisation of America by religious dissenters like the Puritans.
connections: Henry VIII; Protestant Reformation; Elizabeth I; Catholic Church; Charles V

name: Cleopatra, Caesar and Antony
summary: Cleopatra VII used relationships with Rome's two most powerful men to try to save Egypt's independence. Her alliances with Julius Caesar and Mark Antony were political as much as romantic, and they shaped the end of the Roman Republic.
story: According to Plutarch, Cleopatra had herself smuggled into Caesar's quarters in Alexandria in 48 BCE, possibly rolled in a bedroll; she bore him a son, Caesarion. After Caesar's murder she allied with Mark Antony, with whom she had three children. Octavian's propaganda portrayed Antony as enslaved by a foreign seductress, turning Rome against him. After defeat at Actium (31 BCE), both killed themselves.
truth: Roman writers — her enemies — created the image of Cleopatra as a seductive beauty; her coins show a strong nose and plain features. Ancient sources stress instead her intelligence, charm and gift for languages; she was the only Ptolemaic ruler who learned Egyptian.
reshaped: Her defeat made Egypt a Roman province and Octavian became Augustus, the first emperor. Her story has been retold endlessly in plays, films and paintings.
connections: Julius Caesar; Augustus; Ptolemaic Egypt; Roman Republic; Battle of Actium
link_text: Cleopatra VII used relationships with Rome's two most powerful men to try to save Egypt's independence. According to Plutarch, Cleopatra had herself smuggled into Caesar's quarters in Alexandria in 48 BCE, possibly rolled in a bedroll; she bore him a son, Caesarion. After Caesar's murder she allied with Mark Antony, with whom she had three children. Octavian's propaganda portrayed Antony as enslaved by a foreign seductress, turning Rome against him. After defeat at Actium (31 BCE), both killed themselves. Roman writers — her enemies — created the image of Cleopatra as a seductive beauty; her coins show a strong nose and plain features. Ancient sources stress instead her intelligence, charm and gift for languages; she was the only Ptolemaic ruler who learned Egyptian. Her defeat made Egypt a Roman province and Octavian became Augustus, the first emperor. Her story has been retold endlessly in plays, films and paintings. name: Rasputin and the fall of the Romanovs
summary: Grigori Rasputin, a Siberian peasant mystic, gained enormous influence over Tsar Nicholas II and Empress Alexandra because he seemed able to ease the bleeding of their only son Alexei, who had haemophilia. His scandalous reputation for drinking and seducing women helped destroy the monarchy's prestige.
story: Rasputin wandered as a holy man and arrived in St Petersburg in 1903. Brought to the palace in 1905, he calmed Alexei during bleeding crises — perhaps by stopping doctors from giving aspirin, which thins blood, or by calming him. Society women flocked to him, and tales of orgies spread. When Nicholas went to command the army in 1915, Alexandra, guided by Rasputin, appointed and sacked ministers. In December 1916 nobles led by Prince Felix Yusupov lured him to a palace, reportedly fed him poisoned cakes, shot him and threw him into the frozen river.
truth: The legend that poison failed and he survived several shots before drowning comes mainly from Yusupov's dramatic memoir; the autopsy found a fatal shot to the forehead. Rumours that Rasputin was Alexandra's lover were false, but they were believed and printed in cartoons.
reshaped: The scandal made the Romanovs look corrupt and ridiculous at the worst moment of the First World War. Within three months of his murder the Tsar abdicated, leading to the Russian Revolution.

name: Casanova and the libertines
summary: Giacomo Casanova (1725–1798) became so famous for seduction that his name is now a word. But his 3,500-page memoir, History of My Life, is also one of the best pictures of 18th-century European society.
story: The son of Venetian actors, he was in turn a cleric, soldier, violinist, spy, gambler, alchemist and diplomat. Arrested in 1755 by the Venetian Inquisition for 'irreligion', he made a famous escape over the roofs of the Doge's Palace prison in 1756. In Paris he helped set up the French state lottery, became rich and met Voltaire, Benjamin Franklin, Catherine the Great and Mozart's librettist. He spent his last years as a lonely librarian in a Bohemian castle, writing his memoirs.
truth: His memoir describes around 120 lovers — modest by modern celebrity standards — and parts, including relationships with very young girls, are disturbing by any standard. Historians have checked many details and found them surprisingly accurate.
reshaped: Casanova embodied the 'libertine' culture of the Enlightenment aristocracy, which revolutionaries later attacked as decadent. His memoir was only published in full in 1960.
connections: Giacomo Casanova; Enlightenment; Republic of Venice; Voltaire; Catherine the Great

name: Royal mistresses
summary: In many European courts, the king's official mistress (in France, the maîtresse-en-titre) was a political figure with her own apartments, income and influence. The most powerful, Madame de Pompadour, was effectively a minister.
story: Jeanne-Antoinette Poisson, a middle-class Parisian, became Louis XV's mistress in 1745, was made Marquise de Pompadour, and stayed his closest adviser for 20 years. She supported the Encyclopédie of Diderot, the Sèvres porcelain factory, and the 1756 alliance with Austria that led to the Seven Years' War, and influenced appointments of ministers and generals. Her successor, Madame du Barry, was guillotined during the Revolution.
truth: Critics blamed Pompadour for France's defeat in the Seven Years' War, but the alliance was the king's policy. Mistresses were also a sign of how unhappy arranged royal marriages could be.
reshaped: The visible influence of mistresses made the monarchy look corrupt and helped fuel the hatred that led to the French Revolution.
industry: Pompadour's patronage made Sèvres porcelain and Rococo style fashionable across Europe.
connections: Louis XV; French Revolution; Seven Years' War; Enlightenment

name: Harems and the zenana
summary: The harem (Arabic, 'forbidden') or zenana in India was the private women's quarters of a household. In royal palaces it held wives, mothers, concubines, daughters, servants and children, and was guarded by eunuchs — but it was also a centre of political power.
story: In the Ottoman 'Sultanate of Women' (c. 1533–1656), women such as Hürrem Sultan (Roxelana), a slave who became Suleiman the Magnificent's legal wife, and Kösem Sultan effectively ran the empire. Mughal women such as Nur Jahan issued coins and orders in their own names, and Jahanara owned trade ships. Akbar's harem reportedly held about 5,000 women, most of them servants and relatives rather than consorts.
truth: Western painters, who were never allowed inside, imagined harems as erotic places of lounging nude women. In reality most residents were servants and family, and life was governed by strict hierarchy and politics.
reshaped: Harem politics decided successions: Ottoman princes were raised inside the harem and the 'law of fratricide' meant brothers were killed when a new sultan took the throne.
connections: Ottoman Empire; Mughal Empire; Nur Jahan; Akbar; Suleiman the Magnificent; Eunuchs in imperial courts

name: Eunuchs in imperial courts
summary: Eunuchs — castrated men — served as officials, generals and guards in the courts of Assyria, Persia, China, Byzantium, the Islamic world and India for nearly 3,000 years. Because they could not found dynasties, rulers trusted them with power, and some became among the most powerful people of their times.
story: In China eunuchs ran the palace bureaucracy; some, like Cai Lun (credited with inventing paper) and admiral Zheng He, were great achievers, while others, like Wei Zhongxian in the Ming dynasty, terrorised officials. In Delhi, Malik Kafur, a eunuch slave, became Alauddin Khalji's general who conquered the south. The last Chinese imperial eunuchs were expelled from the Forbidden City in 1924.
truth: Many eunuchs were poor boys sold or castrated by their families, and many died from the operation. Their power was often blamed — unfairly as well as fairly — for dynasties' decline.
reshaped: Eunuchs shaped Chinese history, from Han dynasty court coups to Ming naval voyages, and India's hijra communities trace part of their history to the court eunuchs.
connections: Zheng He; Malik Kafur; Ming dynasty; Han dynasty; Byzantine Empire; Castrati; Hijras and Section 377

name: Kama Sutra
summary: The Kama Sutra, written in Sanskrit by Vatsyayana around the 3rd century CE, is famous in the West as a sex manual, but only about a fifth of it deals with sexual positions. It is really a guide to living a cultured, pleasurable life — kama, one of the four aims of Hindu life alongside dharma (duty), artha (wealth) and moksha (liberation).
story: It describes the daily routine of the wealthy urban gentleman (nagaraka): bathing, perfumes, gardens, poetry, music and 64 arts including cooking, chemistry and carpentry. Other books cover choosing a wife, the duties of wives, courtesans, and how to attract partners. It treats women's pleasure as important and discusses women's own desires frankly.
truth: It reached the West through Richard Burton's 1883 translation, published privately by the 'Kama Shastra Society' to dodge Victorian obscenity laws — making it a forbidden best-seller. The famous illustrated editions with paintings are much later Mughal and Rajput works, not part of the original text.
reshaped: The Kama Sutra shows that ancient India discussed sexuality openly as part of a good life, in contrast to later Victorian prudishness that colonial rule helped spread in India. It shaped Western ideas of the 'erotic East'.
industry: It has been reprinted, illustrated and branded endlessly — from coffee-table books to condom brands.
connections: Vatsyayana; Gupta Empire; Hinduism; Khajuraho temples; Victorian era

name: Erotic art of temples and Pompeii
summary: When excavators uncovered Pompeii in the 18th century, they found erotic frescoes, statues and lamps everywhere — in homes, baths, bakeries and a brothel (the Lupanar). Embarrassed authorities locked them in a 'Secret Cabinet' in Naples, open only to 'gentlemen of mature age and respectable morals' until 2000. In India, the temples of Khajuraho and Konark carry carved couples (mithuna) among thousands of other sculptures.
story: Romans saw sexual images as lucky, funny or protective; phallic charms (fascinum) were hung over doorways and on children to ward off the evil eye. At Khajuraho, built by the Chandela dynasty, erotic carvings make up less than a tenth of the sculpture, set among gods, dancers, warriors and daily life. Explanations include tantric symbolism, fertility and auspiciousness, the union of the soul with the divine, and teaching.
truth: The idea that Khajuraho was 'a temple of sex' is a modern tourist myth; and the Victorian reaction to Pompeii told us more about Victorians than Romans. The word 'pornography' itself was coined in the 19th century partly to describe the Pompeii finds.
reshaped: These finds forced Europeans to confront that ancient cultures they admired viewed sex very differently, and shaped modern museum censorship debates.
connections: Pompeii; Khajuraho temples; Konark Sun Temple; Chandela dynasty; Roman Empire; Victorian era

name: Tawaifs of Lucknow
summary: Tawaifs were courtesans of North India, especially Lucknow, Delhi, Benares and Hyderabad, who were above all elite performers of music, dance and poetry. Under the Nawabs of Awadh they were tutors in manners and culture to young nobles, and some were among the wealthiest women in India.
story: They mastered thumri, ghazal, dadra and kathak, and many owned property and paid taxes. Lucknow's tawaifs supported the 1857 rebellion with money and shelter; the British confiscated their property afterward. Colonial law, especially the Contagious Diseases Acts and later anti-nautch campaigns by reformers, recast them simply as prostitutes. In the early 20th century, tawaifs such as Gauhar Jaan became India's first recording stars, and others like Begum Akhtar moved into cinema and radio.
truth: Their world mixed art and sex work, and many entered it through poverty or inheritance; it was neither as glamorous as films like Umrao Jaan and Pakeezah show nor as simple as colonial moralists claimed.
reshaped: Tawaifs preserved and passed on Hindustani classical music and kathak; when they were pushed out, their art was taken up by 'respectable' middle-class performers. Bollywood's courtesan films grew from their memory.
industry: Gauhar Jaan's 1902 records launched India's music recording industry.
connections: Nawabs of Awadh; Indian Rebellion of 1857; Contagious Diseases Acts; Devadasis

name: Devadasis
summary: Devadasis ('servants of god') were girls dedicated to a temple deity, ritually married to the god and trained in dance and music. In the medieval Chola period they were respected artists, and inscriptions record their gifts to temples; the dance form Bharatanatyam developed from their art.
story: The Brihadeeswara temple at Thanjavur supported about 400 temple dancers in the 11th century. Over time, with temples losing royal patronage, many devadasis came to depend on patrons, and the system became linked with concubinage and sex work. British officials and Indian reformers like Muthulakshmi Reddy campaigned against it; Madras banned dedications in 1947, Karnataka in 1982 and Andhra in 1988.
truth: Dedication of girls, often from Dalit families, continues illegally in parts of Karnataka, Maharashtra and Andhra Pradesh, where it amounts to trafficking. Reformers also erased a living art tradition, which was then 'revived' by upper-caste performers like Rukmini Devi Arundale.
reshaped: The abolition debate became one of early Indian feminism's major battles, and Bharatanatyam became India's national 'classical' dance.
connections: Chola dynasty; Brihadeeswara Temple; Tawaifs of Lucknow; Caste system

name: Geisha
summary: Geisha ('person of the arts') are Japanese entertainers trained for years in music, dance, conversation and the tea ceremony. The first geisha in the 18th century were actually men, and women soon took over the profession.
story: Geisha worked in pleasure districts like Kyoto's Gion, entertaining wealthy clients at banquets, separate from the licensed courtesans (oiran). Apprentices (maiko) trained from childhood; at their peak in the 1920s there were about 80,000 geisha. Today there are only around 1,000.
truth: Western soldiers after 1945 confused geisha with prostitutes, partly because some sex workers called themselves 'geisha girls'. The practice of mizuage — auctioning an apprentice's virginity — existed before it was outlawed in 1959, and memoirs like Mineko Iwasaki's dispute how common it was.
reshaped: Geisha preserved traditional Japanese arts and became a global symbol of Japan.
connections: Edo period; Japan; Tokugawa shogunate

name: Courtly love and troubadours
summary: In 12th-century Occitania, poet-musicians called troubadours invented the idea of romantic love in European literature: a knight devoted to an unattainable noble lady, often married to someone else, serving and adoring her from afar.
story: Duke William IX of Aquitaine was the first known troubadour; his granddaughter Eleanor of Aquitaine and her daughter Marie de Champagne made their courts centres of the new culture. The Arthurian romances of Lancelot and Guinevere spread the ideals across Europe.
truth: Scholars still argue whether 'courtly love' was ever practised or just a literary game; some trace its ideas to Arabic poetry from Al-Andalus.
reshaped: Courtly love shaped Western ideas of romance, chivalry and love marriages, which eventually displaced arranged marriages in the West.
industry: Its ideals lie behind romance novels and Valentine's Day, which became a commercial holiday in the 19th century.
connections: Eleanor of Aquitaine; Al-Andalus; Knights; Middle Ages

name: Comstock laws
summary: The Comstock Act of 1873 made it a federal crime in the USA to send 'obscene' material through the mail — including contraceptives, information about birth control and abortion, and medical textbooks.
story: Anthony Comstock, a dry-goods clerk turned anti-vice crusader, became a postal inspector and boasted of destroying 15 tons of books and causing 15 suicides. Margaret Sanger was charged under the law for her pamphlets.
truth: Parts of the Comstock Act were never repealed and became part of US abortion debates again after 2022.
reshaped: It drove birth control underground for nearly a century and made censorship a central fight in American culture.
connections: Margaret Sanger; The birth-control pill; Contraception before the Pill

name: Contagious Diseases Acts
summary: Worried that venereal disease was weakening the army and navy, Britain passed laws letting police register any woman suspected of being a prostitute in garrison towns and force her to undergo genital examinations; women found infected could be locked in 'lock hospitals' for months. Soldiers were not examined.
story: Josephine Butler led a campaign arguing the laws punished women for men's behaviour, and the acts were repealed in Britain in 1886. In India, cantonment regulations created regimental brothels and forced inspection of Indian women, and registered tawaifs as prostitutes.
truth: The laws did little to reduce disease, but they made the state the controller of women's bodies.
reshaped: Butler's campaign became one of the first mass feminist movements and inspired the fight for women's votes.
connections: Tawaifs of Lucknow; British Raj; Women's suffrage; Syphilis

name: Hijras and Section 377
summary: Section 377 of the Indian Penal Code, written by Thomas Macaulay's commission in 1860 and in force from 1862, criminalised 'carnal intercourse against the order of nature', and was used against gay men and transgender people for over 150 years.
story: Hijras — a transgender and intersex community with a recorded history going back to ancient texts and Mughal courts — were labelled a 'criminal tribe' by the British in 1871. After decades of activism, India's Supreme Court recognised transgender people as a 'third gender' in 2014, and in Navtej Singh Johar v. Union of India (6 September 2018) it struck down Section 377 for consensual adults.
truth: Similar British laws remain in many former colonies; ancient Indian texts describe 'third nature' (tritiya prakriti) people without criminalising them.
reshaped: The 2018 ruling transformed LGBTQ life in India and influenced other former British colonies.
connections: British Raj; Criminal Tribes Act; Eunuchs in imperial courts; Stonewall riots

After decades of activism, India's Supreme Court recognised transgender people as a 'third gender' in 2014, and in Navtej Singh Johar v. Union of India (6 September 2018) it struck down Section 377 for consensual adults. Similar British laws remain in many former colonies; ancient Indian texts describe 'third nature' (tritiya prakriti) people without criminalising them. The 2018 ruling transformed LGBTQ life in India and influenced other former British colonies.  British Raj; Criminal Tribes Act; Eunuchs in imperial courts; Stonewall riots India

name: Oscar Wilde and Alan Turing
summary: Two of Britain's greatest minds were destroyed by laws against homosexuality. Playwright Oscar Wilde was sentenced to two years' hard labour in 1895, and codebreaker Alan Turing was convicted in 1952 and forced to take hormones.
story: Wilde sued the Marquess of Queensberry for libel after being called a sodomite; the case collapsed and he was prosecuted under the 1885 Labouchere Amendment. Prison broke his health and he died in Paris in 1900. Turing, whose work cracking the Enigma code helped win WWII, was given 'chemical castration' with oestrogen instead of prison, lost his security clearance and died of cyanide poisoning in 1954.
truth: About 75,000 men were convicted under such laws in England and Wales. Britain pardoned them, including Turing, in 2013–2017 ('Turing's Law').
reshaped: These cases became symbols of injustice that helped decriminalise homosexuality in England in 1967.
connections: Alan Turing; Victorian era; World War II; Stonewall riots

name: Stonewall riots
summary: When police raided the Stonewall Inn, a gay bar in New York, patrons and locals fought back for several nights. The riots are seen as the start of the modern gay-rights movement.
story: Police raids on gay bars were routine; this time drag queens, trans women, lesbians and street youth resisted. A year later the first Pride marches commemorated the event, now held in June worldwide.
truth: Who threw the 'first brick' is disputed, and trans women of colour such as Marsha P. Johnson and Sylvia Rivera were long left out of the story.
reshaped: Pride, same-sex marriage (first legal in the Netherlands, 2001) and LGBTQ rights movements across the world trace their origins here.
industry: Pride became a major commercial and tourism event.
connections: Sexual revolution; AIDS crisis and activism; Hijras and Section 377

name: Magdalene laundries
summary: Catholic religious orders in Ireland ran institutions where 'fallen women' — unmarried mothers, girls thought too flirtatious, victims of abuse — were locked up and made to work unpaid in commercial laundries.
story: About 30,000 women passed through, some for life. Babies of unmarried mothers were taken from them and many were adopted abroad, often to the USA. The last laundry closed in 1996.
truth: In 1993 a mass grave of 155 women was found at a laundry site. The Irish state apologised in 2013, and investigations of mother-and-baby homes found that about 9,000 children died in them.
reshaped: The scandals collapsed the authority of the Catholic Church in Ireland, which then legalised same-sex marriage (2015) and abortion (2018) by referendum.
connections: Catholic Church; Ireland

name: Comfort women
summary: The Japanese military forced an estimated 50,000 to 200,000 women and girls — mainly from Korea, but also China, the Philippines, Indonesia and elsewhere — into sexual slavery in military brothels called 'comfort stations'.
story: Women were recruited by deception, sold or kidnapped. Many died or were killed; survivors stayed silent for decades out of shame. In 1991 Kim Hak-sun became the first to testify publicly.
truth: Japan's 1993 Kono Statement acknowledged military involvement, but some Japanese politicians still deny coercion. Statues of comfort women remain a source of diplomatic disputes.
reshaped: Their testimony helped make wartime sexual violence prosecutable as a crime against humanity.
connections: World War II; Nanjing Massacre; Empire of Japan; Korea

name: Sexual revolution
summary: In the 1960s and 70s Western attitudes to sex changed faster than at any time in history: sex before marriage became normal, divorce easier, censorship weaker and gay and women's rights movements rose.
story: Drivers included the Pill, rising education, youth culture, the Kinsey reports, and magazines like Hugh Hefner's Playboy (1953). Courts struck down obscenity bans on books like Lady Chatterley's Lover (1960 in Britain).
truth: Critics from the left and right argued that the revolution mostly benefited men, or weakened family stability; its gains also arrived very unevenly across the world.
reshaped: It changed family life, marriage and fashion; divorce rates, single parenthood and cohabitation rose.
industry: Pornography, sex education, dating and later online platforms became huge industries.
connections: The birth-control pill; Kinsey Reports; Stonewall riots; Feminism

name: Online dating
summary: Matchmaking moved from families, marriage brokers and newspaper adverts to the internet with Match.com (1995), then apps like Grindr (2009) and Tinder (2012) with its swipe.
story: By the late 2010s meeting online was the most common way US couples met. In India matrimonial sites like Shaadi.com (1997) digitised arranged marriage.
truth: Dating apps have been linked to scams, discrimination and harassment, and their algorithms shape who meets whom.
reshaped: It widened people's pool of partners, increased marriages across communities, and changed social life.
industry: Online dating earns over $9 billion a year.
connections: Information Age; Internet
